articles.title: St Cuthbert's RC High School launches new garden project
articles.excerpt: St Cuthbert's RC High School in Rochdale has unveiled a new garden project aimed at enhancing outdoor learning for students.
articles.content_html:
St Cuthbert's RC High School in Rochdale has launched a new garden project to enhance outdoor learning for students. The initiative was announced on 10 November 2026, showcasing the school's commitment to providing a vibrant space for students.

The garden will serve as an educational resource, allowing students to engage with nature and learn about gardening and sustainability. This project is part of the school's broader efforts to improve outdoor facilities for its students.

A spokesperson for St Cuthbert's RC High School said: "This garden will not only beautify our school but also provide a hands-on learning experience for our students."

The project aligns with the school's educational goals and community engagement initiatives, fostering a sense of responsibility and care for the environment among students.

articles.title: Rochdale Christmas Toy Appeal opens for donations after helping 3,000 children last year
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Christmas Toy Appeal is now accepting donations until 11 December, aiming to support local children in need this festive season.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale Christmas Toy Appeal has opened for donations, aiming to support local children in need this festive season. The appeal, which has been running since 2013, helped 3,000 children last year and is now accepting gifts until 11 December.

Donations are being collected for children aged up to 16 and can be left at various local libraries and leisure centres. Additional collection points include Rochdale Riverside and The Trade Centre UK, making it easier for residents to contribute.

Organised in partnership with local charities and organisations, the appeal encourages the community to shop locally and choose sustainable gifts. Council volunteers will distribute the collected gifts before Christmas Day, ensuring they reach those who need them most.

Requests for help have already been received this year, highlighting the ongoing need for support within the community. The collaborative effort aims to bring joy to local families during the festive period.

articles.excerpt: The shortlist for the Raising Rochdale Education Awards 2026 has been revealed, celebrating local educators' contributions to children's lives.
articles.content_html:
The shortlist for this year’s Raising Rochdale Education Awards has been announced, recognising the outstanding contributions of local educators.

The awards ceremony will take place on Friday, 20 November 2026, at Rochdale Town Hall, celebrating the achievements of teachers, tutors, support staff, and other education professionals.

This year, a record 896 nominations were submitted, highlighting the dedication of those who work to give children and young people the best start in life.

Eighteen awards will be presented, including categories such as Raising Rochdale School or College of the Year and Leadership Team of the Year.

Event organiser Andrew Bridson, headteacher of Cardinal Langley RC High School, expressed excitement about the event, stating, "We are thrilled to celebrate the incredible work of our educators and the positive impact they have on the lives of children and young people."

The Raising Rochdale Education Awards, now in its third year, aims to honour those who contribute significantly to education in the borough. Winners will be announced in front of a packed audience of local education professionals, sponsors, family, and friends.

The outcome of the court appearance on 4 January will determine the next steps in this case, as the legal proceedings continue. Rochdale Daily has asked Greater Manchester Police for comment.

articles.title: CEAMS wins national award for sustainable manufacturing innovation
articles.excerpt: The Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) has received national recognition for its innovative work in recycling carbon fibre.
articles.content_html:
The Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) has won the Sustainability and Circularity Award at the Composites UK Industry Awards for its pioneering work in recycling carbon fibre, marking a significant achievement for the Rochdale-based initiative.

In collaboration with partners including Cygnet Texkimp, SHD Composites, NCC, and Teledyne CML Composites, CEAMS demonstrated a world-first aerospace component made from prepreg material containing 100% recycled continuous carbon fibre.

This innovation proves that recycled carbon fibre can achieve stiffness and strength comparable to virgin materials while utilising existing manufacturing processes.

Rochdale Development Agency, a founding partner of CEAMS, expressed pride in supporting such innovative projects that address real-world challenges. The agency highlighted that this award reinforces Rochdale's growing reputation as a hub for advanced manufacturing and sustainable industry, contributing to the future economy.

Previous research by CEAMS indicated that using recycled continuous carbon fibre could reduce carbon emissions by up to 80% compared to virgin materials.

Donations for the appeal can be made until 11 December 2026, at various local libraries and leisure centres across the borough.

The council's initiative is a response to the growing number of requests for help from families, making it crucial for many during the holiday season.

articles.title: Dunelm Rochdale shoppers fill store with Christmas gifts for Delivering Joy appeal
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale store says customers have dropped off so many presents in the past week that staff are preparing a count. Gifts go to local causes for people who might otherwise go without.
articles.content_html:
Shoppers at Dunelm's Rochdale store have dropped off so many Christmas presents for its Delivering Joy appeal that staff are preparing to count them up.

The store has thanked customers for the gifts left over the past week, which will go to people in the community who might otherwise go without at Christmas.

In a message to customers, the Rochdale store said: “We’ve had sooooo many gifts dropped off in store over the past week by lots of lovely customers – thank you so much for taking part, you are all so thoughtful & generous! We can’t wait to do a count up to see how many gifts we have now!”

Delivering Joy, which returned on 13 October, is now in its seventh year. Shoppers pick up a gift tag in store, buy a present and leave it at the store, which passes the gifts on to local causes.

Last year the homeware retailer donated nearly 200,000 gifts to more than 1,500 local causes across its stores, according to Dunelm.

Gift bags must be left unsealed so staff can check the contents before the presents are delivered.

If the tags have run out, shoppers can still take part by donating to Age UK, either online at dunelm.com or in store by taking an Age UK bauble to the till and giving anything from £1 to £100.

articles.title: Is Rochdale Town Hall haunted?
articles.excerpt: There is no verified evidence that the Town Hall is haunted — but its Victorian courts, an 1883 fire, local poltergeist tales and commercial ghost-hunt events have kept the rumours alive.
articles.summary: There is no verified evidence that the Town Hall is haunted — but its Victorian courts, an 1883 fire, local poltergeist tales and commercial ghost-hunt events have kept the rumours alive.
articles.body:
Short answer: no confirmed haunting has been proved.

Rochdale Town Hall is a Grade I Victorian building with a long, well‑documented civic history; that history — not a stack of authenticated supernatural incidents — is what official records record. The council and the Town Hall’s own conservation pages describe the building’s architect (William Henry Crossland), its opening in 1871, the destructive 1883 fire that brought down the original spire and the major restoration work in the 2020s that reopened previously closed rooms to the public. Those are the facts you can rely on. (Rochdale Borough Council and the Town Hall’s conservation pages do not present any official claims of ghosts.)

So where do the hauntings come from? Two things make the building fertile ground for ghost stories. First, old civic buildings commonly held grim functions: magistrates’ hearings, police business and holding cells have been associated with many town halls across the region, and such associations encourage mobile storytelling about restless spirits. Second, modern interest in the paranormal has been channelled into commercial events. Organisers such as Haunted Happenings advertise overnight “ghost hunts” at Rochdale Town Hall, offering vigils, equipment and guided investigations. Those events are available to book and are the clearest public evidence that people believe the building is worth investigating for ghostly activity — but they are promotions by private operators, not independent, peer‑reviewed proof of anything supernatural.

It is important to separate three things: documented history, local folklore and commercial claims. Documented history (architecture, dates, the 1883 fire, the recent conservation programme) is recorded by the Town Hall and its conservation partners and by national heritage bodies. Local folklore includes older regional tales — Rochdale borough has other well‑known legends and alleged poltergeist cases (for example reported mid‑20th century household disturbances in the Kirkholt area) — but those stories are about people and places across the borough, not verified phenomena inside the Town Hall itself. Commercial claims are where the line blurs: ghost‑hunting companies and enthusiast sites promote investigations and recount experiences, but those accounts are not the same as corroborated evidence assessed by historians or independent investigators.

If you want to check the official record: Historic and civic sources list the building, its architecture and its conservation programme; Rochdale Borough Council and the Town Hall’s visitor pages outline opening times, the recent restoration and the cultural uses of the Great Hall and other rooms. If you want to see the building after dark, private operators run ticketed paranormal events; those operators describe the kinds of activities they run and their booking rules on their commercial pages. Neither the council nor the Town Hall’s official material presents verified sightings, authenticated recordings or formal investigations that demonstrate the presence of spirits.

What this means for locals: you can enjoy the building’s architecture, visit the Great Hall, watch the peregrine falcons nest in the clock tower via the Town Hall webcam, attend a concert or book a wedding there with confidence that the publicly recorded history is well maintained. If you’re tempted by a ghost hunt, treat it as an experience — a themed night in an atmospheric historic setting — rather than settled proof. Where claims are important to people (for example, allegations of harm or historical abuse) always rely on official findings; nothing we found links such matters to hauntings at the Town Hall.

If you’d like to follow up: the Town Hall’s official history and conservation information are the best starting point; the council’s events and visitor pages give current opening arrangements and services. For those curious about local folklore beyond the Town Hall, compiled reports and archives record several separate local poltergeist and haunting tales — interesting as social history, but not evidence of an institutional haunting in the Town Hall itself.

In short: the Town Hall’s drama is historical and architectural. The ghosts are, so far as the record shows, a matter of local legend, private experience and commercial entertainment, not established public fact.

articles.title: School-run parking in Rochdale: what can the council do?
articles.excerpt: The council has stepped up patrols outside schools and is consulting on School Streets. New pavement parking powers are on the way from the government.
articles.content_html:
Parents across the borough who face double-parked cars, blocked crossings and mounted pavements at the school gates every morning have more options than they may think.

Rochdale Borough Council launched its Stop Means Stop campaign at St Luke's Primary School in Heywood on 28 September, telling drivers to stop for school crossing patrols.

The council recorded 137 cases over the past five years of drivers failing to stop outside schools, including cases where a crossing patrol had already stepped into the road.

It said parking enforcement patrols outside schools would increase, with no fixed schedule, and asked drivers to keep yellow lines and school keep-clear markings free.

Councillor Dylan Williams, cabinet member for highways and facilities, said: “It's really important that people stop.” He described the risk as “a real danger for schoolchildren across the borough.”

A crossing patrol worker at St Luke's said cars parked on the zigzag lines blocked his view and the view of passing drivers.

One longer-term answer is a School Street. These schemes restrict vehicles on the road outside a school at drop-off and pick-up times, so it becomes a space for people walking, cycling or scooting.

Residents, Blue Badge holders, healthcare workers and the emergency services can be given exemptions, according to the council. A School Street can only go ahead with the school's backing, and schools or communities register interest through Transport for Greater Manchester.

The council has consulted on a School Street trial at Smithy Bridge Primary School in Littleborough, with a consultation that ran from 27 November 2025 to 16 January 2026. No decision has been published.

Pavement parking is the other common complaint. On 8 January, the Department for Transport announced that councils in England would get powers to restrict pavement parking across wider areas, rather than street by street.

Local transport minister Lilian Greenwood said: “Clear pavements are essential for people to move around safely and independently.” The department said guidance on using the powers would be published later in 2026.

Since July 2023 the council has also held powers to fine drivers caught on camera committing moving traffic offences, such as blocking yellow box junctions and making banned turns.

Problem parking outside a school can be reported to the council's Parking Services at ParkingServices@rochdale.gov.uk or on 0300 303 8879, Monday to Friday, 8.30am to 4.45pm. Dangerous driving should be reported to Greater Manchester Police on 101 or online, or 999 in an emergency.

articles.title: Cranmer Education Trust staff gather for professional development event
articles.excerpt: Staff from Cranmer Education Trust, which operates schools in Middleton and Oldham, convened for a professional development event aimed at improving children's lives through inclusive education.
articles.content_html:
Staff from Cranmer Education Trust gathered for a professional development event called Belong 26 at The Blue Coat School and The Loom in Oldham, aimed at enhancing children's educational experiences.

The event brought together teaching and support staff from the trust's ten schools, including St John’s CE Primary School and Rhodes Green CE Primary School in Middleton.

The focus of Belong 26 was on fostering high expectations, strong relationships, and shared expertise to ensure every child has the opportunity to flourish.

The trust's schools cater to more than 7,500 children and young people across Oldham and Rochdale, prioritising excellence and inclusion in education.

During the event, staff participated in practical workshops covering topics such as inclusive teaching, attendance, safeguarding, and communication. These workshops aimed to equip educators with the tools necessary to understand and address the challenges faced by students, helping them overcome barriers to learning and achievement.

Cranmer Education Trust believes that maintaining high expectations for every child is essential for their success. The collaborative efforts of the staff at Belong 26 reflect a commitment to improving educational outcomes for all students.

Teaching and support staff from across Cranmer Education Trust came together for Belong 26, a trust-wide professional development event dedicated to strengthening inclusive education and ensuring every child has the opportunity to flourish. Last week’s event at The Blue Coat School and The Loom in Oldham, brought together colleagues from the trust’s ten schools, including teachers, teaching assistants, school leaders, pastoral teams, business, technical and operational staff, including St John’s CE Primary School in Middleton, Rhodes Green CE Primary School Rhodes and St Anne’s CE Academy in Middleton. Business and technical colleagues considered how everyday systems, processes and communications can either remove barriers or unintentionally create them. articles.title: Rochdale man who managed 'Adam' drug line dealers jailed for 10 and a half years
articles.excerpt: Haider Ali, 34, of Pike Street, was sentenced at Minshull Street Crown Court on Monday 9 November after an investigation that began with a drug deal on Baron Street.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale man who rose from street dealer to manager in the organised crime group behind the borough's 'Adam' drug line has been jailed for 10 years and six months.

Haider Ali, 34, of Pike Street, Rochdale, was sentenced at Minshull Street Crown Court on Monday 9 November 2026.

He was sentenced for being concerned in the supply of cocaine and of heroin, and two counts each of possession with intent to supply cocaine and heroin, covering September 2024 to March 2025.

The investigation by GMP's Rochdale Challenger Unit began after police received information that a drug deal had taken place from a car parked on Baron Street, in Rochdale town centre, just before midnight on 4 January 2025.

Officers followed the vehicle and carried out a reinforced stop when it pulled into a local petrol station. Ali, a passenger, got out and walked quickly away before he was detained.

He was found with more than £1,000 in cash and two mobile phones, which were seized.

In custody, officers recovered two bundles of wraps containing a brown and a white substance, later confirmed as heroin and cocaine. A pre-paid phone taken from him was confirmed to be the Adam drug line.

Investigators found Ali was not only dealing at street level but managing other street dealers, the dedicated dealer phone, and where those below him should make their next deal.

A warrant was executed at his home on 27 March 2025, when he was arrested again on suspicion of possession with intent to supply class A drugs and being concerned in their supply.

PC Joe Cooke, of GMP's Rochdale Challenger Unit, said: “The ‘Adam’ Organised Crime Group have caused misery for many years to the residents and communities of Rochdale and beyond. Haider Ali’s drug dealing as part of this OCG and his management of lower-level street dealers has contributed significantly to the success of the Adam OCG.”

He added: “Organised criminals such as Haider Ali are dangerous individuals with no remorse for their criminality. They operate to exploit the most vulnerable in our societies in order to increase their financial gain and notoriety.”

According to police, evidence showed Ali had progressed from street dealing in 2014 to a significant role within the Adam group by 2024 and into 2025.

Concerns about drug dealing can be reported to GMP on 101 or online at www.gmp.police.uk, or anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

articles.title: Police warn Rochdale homes to lock away family gold after rise in burglaries
articles.excerpt: Burglaries targeting family gold have risen in Rochdale, Oldham and Bury in recent weeks, mostly at weekends, with entry usually gained at the rear of homes.
articles.content_html:
Police are urging Rochdale households to lock away family gold and jewellery after a rise in burglaries targeting it in Rochdale, Oldham and Bury in recent weeks.

Greater Manchester Police said the burglaries have mostly taken place at weekends, during the late afternoon and at night, and warned that offences are likely to increase as the darker nights draw in.

Burglars have most often got in by snapping or tampering with locks or by smashing their way in, while some properties were entered because they had been left insecure.

Entry is typically gained at the rear of the property. Police believe the offenders' vehicle is usually parked on streets surrounding the targeted home.

Detective Chief Inspector Roger Smethurst, of GMP's Serious Crime Division, said: "I would like to remind the public to stay vigilant as the darker nights draw in and ensure their property is secure.

"Anyone with expensive jewellery in their homes should ensure it is safely locked away, out of sight, purchasing a good quality safe which complies with insurance rating standards."

The warning comes as GMP reports that it has been the country's top force for solving residential burglaries over the last 12 months.

The force said 14.3% of residential burglaries so far this year have been solved, up from 9.5% the previous year.

In August 2026 alone, 15.9% of residential burglary outcomes were solved, compared with 9.8% in August 2025, according to GMP.

Crime prevention advice is available on the Greater Manchester Police website, gmp.police.uk.

Suspicious activity or information can be reported to GMP on 101, or anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

Source: Greater Manchester Police, supplied to Rochdale Daily. Photograph: Greater Manchester Police (stock image).

articles.title: Wirral thrash Rochdale 46-0 in rugby match
articles.excerpt: Wirral secured a dominant 46-0 victory over Rochdale, moving up to third in the league table ahead of their next match against Leek.
articles.content_html:
Wirral secured a commanding 46-0 victory over Rochdale in a rugby match on Saturday, marking their sixth win in seven games and propelling them to third place in the league table.

The match took place on a pitch ideal for open rugby, with Wirral dominating the early stages.

They opened the scoring in the 12th minute through leading try scorer Tom Akehurst, followed by four more tries before half-time, including contributions from Jacob Mitchell, Will Morris, and Nkateko Phakula, who scored on his debut. At half-time, the score stood at 29-0.

In the second half, Rochdale showed more resilience, attempting to break through Wirral's defence. However, Wirral continued their scoring spree with tries from Adam Don, Rhys James, and Zane Pretorius, adding one more conversion to finish the match at 46-0.

This result leaves Wirral in a strong position as they prepare for their next match against Leek on 21 November at the Memorial Ground.

Wirral's victory not only boosts their league standing but also highlights their strong form as they face three of the top four teams in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Rochdale fighter Owen Webster loses BKFC bout in Glasgow but keeps the town behind him
articles.excerpt: Webster was stopped by Dan Morel in the fourth round at the OVO Hydro on Saturday and has thanked the fans who travelled, saying he will be back better than ever.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale bare-knuckle fighter Owen Webster has thanked the fans who travelled to Glasgow to support him, after losing his BKFC bout to Dan Morel on Saturday night.

Morel won the featherweight contest at the OVO Hydro on Saturday 7 November by technical knockout in the fourth round, stopping Webster 1 minute 17 seconds into the round.

The fight was part of the Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship's BKFC 96 card in Glasgow.

Webster said afterwards: “Nothing in life is easy and if it is it ain't worth it. Saturday night just wasn't meant to be there's no excuses Dan was just the better man on the night and I take my hat off to him.”

He added: “This isn't the end of my journey it's just the beginning theirs a bigger plan for me and I'm sure of that.”

Webster thanked supporters who made the trip to Scotland and those who watched at home, saying: “The love I have for every one of you is unbelievable.”

He also thanked his sponsors for backing him through his fight camps and career, and BKFC for giving him a place on what he called one of the greatest cards in history.

He said he would now take time to heal before returning, adding: “Like I said I'll be back better than ever.”

articles.title: Comment: Should fireworks be allowed on any night but bonfire night?
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's council displays went quiet this year, but residents say fireworks carried on into this week. We look at the law, the harm to people and animals, and what could change.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council chose reduced-noise fireworks for its three bonfire events this year, yet residents say the bangs have carried on well into this week. Is it time to ask whether fireworks should be allowed on any night other than bonfire night?

The council's displays ran on Monday 2 November in Middleton, Tuesday 3 November in Heywood and Wednesday 4 November at Cronkeyshaw Common. None fell on Thursday 5 November itself.

By most accounts the Cronkeyshaw display worked: an eyewitness told Rochdale Daily that the quieter, music-led fireworks were enjoyed by a large crowd with little traffic disruption.

The problem is what happens outside the organised events. Residents have reported fireworks through the weekend and into Monday, after the council displays and bonfire night had both passed.

This is not new. In July and August, households in Shawclough and Healey reported explosions after 11pm on consecutive nights, with parents describing children woken after bedtime and pet owners describing distressed animals.

At full council on 15 October, Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short raised residents' concerns about fireworks being used throughout the year. Councillor Tricia Ayrton said she had been speaking with partner agencies about a coordinated response, and encouraged councillors to raise the call for stronger national action with their MPs.

What the law actually says

In England, adult fireworks may not be set off between 11pm and 7am under the Fireworks Regulations 2004. The exceptions are bonfire night, when the cut-off is midnight, and New Year's Eve, Diwali and the first day of Chinese New Year, when it is 1am. Council-run and national celebration displays are also exempt.

Outside those nights, nothing stops a private display at 10.59pm on any evening of the year.

Shops without an all-year licence may sell to the public only from 15 October to 10 November, from 26 to 31 December, and in the days before Diwali and Chinese New Year. Retailers with a council licence can sell all year round. Consumer fireworks are capped at 120 decibels, and it is an offence to sell adult fireworks to under-18s.

The curfew is enforced by the police, and breaches can bring a fine of up to £5,000. In practice, proving who lit a firework in a back garden at 11.30pm is difficult, and a short burst of noise rarely meets the threshold for a council statutory nuisance investigation.

Scotland has gone further. The Fireworks and Pyrotechnic Articles (Scotland) Act 2022 restricts public use to 6pm to 11pm, with later cut-offs on the main celebration nights, and lets councils designate firework control zones where fireworks are banned at all times.

The physical harm

NHS England figures reported last month showed 161 firework-related hospital admissions in England in 2025, up from 120 the year before. November alone accounted for 85 admissions, compared with 60 in November 2024.

In 2019 a coalition of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons, the British Society for Surgery of the Hand and the British Burn Association reported 1,936 A&E visits for firework injuries in a single year. Hand surgeons said they often treat people who have lost large portions of a hand, and children made up 31% of admissions.

The coalition pointed to Northern Ireland, where licensing for the more powerful categories of firework was followed by reported injuries falling from 136 in 2001 to 38 in 2002.

Pets, livestock and wildlife

In the RSPCA's 2024 impact survey, 66% of respondents said backyard displays were a major concern. The charity wants consumer fireworks cut from 120 to 90 decibels, sales limited to licensed shops, and firework-free zones near animals and vulnerable people.

The horse charity Redwings gathered more than 45,000 signatures in seven weeks last year for the same 90-decibel limit.

The National Farmers' Union says sudden explosions are one of the main causes of stress and injury in livestock, and has reported a member losing around four acres of wheat to a stray firework. The borough's Pennine farmland sits close to housing in Littleborough, Milnrow and Norden.

Researchers at Anglia Ruskin University reported last year that crows, rooks and jackdaws abandoned their roosts and flew erratically on New Year's Eve, which the authors linked to prolonged stress.

People with PTSD and anxiety

Help for Heroes and Combat Stress surveyed veterans in 2023. Almost a quarter (23%) said fireworks had triggered a negative experience, from feeling jumpy to panic attacks. Some 74% wanted the days and times fireworks can be used restricted further, and 67% wanted fewer days on which they can be sold.

Unannounced displays on ordinary nights give anyone with an anxiety condition no chance to prepare.

Weddings and New Year

Weddings sit in an awkward place. There is no special rule for them: a wedding display follows the same 11pm curfew as any other private use, on any night of the year, using fireworks from an all-year licensed seller.

For the couple it is one night. For neighbours, a busy wedding season can mean several unplanned displays a month, with no warning.

New Year's Eve is already protected in law until 1am, and few would argue against a midnight countdown. The question is whether the nights either side of it, and of bonfire night, should be treated the same way.

The case against tighter rules

There are serious arguments on the other side. Most people who use fireworks do so legally and safely, and displays are a valued part of family celebrations, religious festivals such as Diwali, and community fundraising.

The NFU itself opposes a complete ban on consumer fireworks, preferring quieter products and advance notice for farms. Opponents of tighter rules also argue that restricting legal sales could push buyers towards unsafe, unregulated products. And the curfew is already widely broken, so a stricter law with the same weak enforcement may change little.

What could be done

The Government's consultation, which closed on 7 October 2026, asked whether the consumer noise limit should fall from 120 decibels to 110, 100 or 90, and proposed reserving the loudest fireworks for professional displays. It did not propose limiting the nights on which fireworks can be used, and its response has not yet been published.

Options that would go further include:

Restricting private use to bonfire night, New Year's Eve and recognised religious festivals, with all-year use limited to licensed and notified displays.

Ending or tightening all-year retail licences, so that fireworks are not on sale in July and August.

Requiring advance notice to neighbours and nearby farms for wedding and private displays outside the permitted nights.

Giving English councils the same power as Scottish councils to create firework-free zones around farms, nature reserves such as Healey Dell, and care homes.

Making quieter fireworks, like those used at Cronkeyshaw, the standard for consumer sale.

Rochdale has already shown that a council display can be quieter and still draw a crowd. Whether the rules for everyone else should follow is a decision for Parliament, including the MPs who represent the borough.

Fireworks used after 11pm on non-permitted nights can be reported to Greater Manchester Police on 101 or online.

Sources: Fireworks Regulations 2004; Rochdale Borough Council; Department for Business and Trade consultation (July 2026); NHS England via ITV News; BAPRAS, BSSH and British Burn Association; RSPCA; Redwings; National Farmers' Union; Anglia Ruskin University; Help for Heroes and Combat Stress; Scottish Government. No previous experience is needed, and full training is provided in safeguarding, vulnerability awareness and conflict management. Volunteers must be 16 or over and can help regularly or occasionally.
